Army Technical Sgt. Don Halverson and five other World War II veterans will be honored during an Aug. 18 dinner cruise on the St. Croix River to benefit the Stillwater Veterans Memorial. Army Technical Sgt. Don Halverson, 103, of Brooklyn Center, pictured in Italy in 1945 after the end of World War II, will be honored during an Aug. 18, 2026, dinner cruise on the St. Croix River to benefit the Stillwater Veterans Memorial. (Courtesy of Thomas Halvorson) Halverson, 103, of Brooklyn Center, joined the U.S. Army in 1943. He was assigned to the 34th Infantry Division Red Bull unit and led a platoon of soldiers from Naples, Italy, to the border of Switzerland. He was present when the German 34th Division surrendered to the American 34th Infantry Division on May 2, 1945, and he received a citation recognizing this historical event. Halverson also was awarded the Bronze Star, The Good Conduct medal, the Distinguished Unit Badge, the Combat Infantry Badge and the European African Middle Eastern Theater Ribbon. Later in life, he received the Order of St. Maurice medal and the Order of St. George Medallion. Other WWII veterans who will be honored include Ed Albrecht, 101; Bob Holmstrom, 100; Jim Rasmussen, 102; Bill Kruschel, 101, and Bob Michelsen, 100. Also attending will be Holocaust survivor Cass Lewart, 96, who survived a Warsaw ghetto as a 14-year-old youth, said John Kraemer, a member of the Stillwater Veterans Memorial board. This year’s featured speaker is retired U.S. Marine Corps Col. John Kline, who served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2003 to 2017. Proceeds will fund operations, maintenance and future expansion of the veterans memorial site at Third and Pine streets, Kraemer said. Tickets are $35; reservations are required. Boarding of the Avalon starts at 4:30 p.m. at Stillwater River Boats, 525 S. Main St., with departure at 5:45 p.m. and return from the round trip to Hudson, Wis., by 8 p.m. The program includes a buffet dinner, cash bar, raffles and opportunities for guests to visit with veterans. https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/topical-i.text: The number of teaching vacancies in Slovakia has fallen by 31 percent year on year. But schools are still struggling to find teachers. According to data from the Edujobs job portal, primary and secondary schools across the country are currently looking to fill 343 teaching positions. The biggest shortage is in the Bratislava Region, with 137 vacancies, while the fewest are in the Žilina Region, with just 13. The disparity is largely linked to the higher cost of living in the capital. Education Minister Tomáš Drucker (HLAS-SD) says that in areas where schools struggle to attract teachers, they are competing with other professions offering better salaries. Therefore, teachers in Bratislava, Trnava and Košice receive additional monthly payments to help bridge the gap. Demand also varies by subject. While schools are struggling to find teachers of subjects such as mathematics and English, there is an oversupply of physical education teachers. According to Pavel Ondek, Chairman of the Education Workers’ Trade Union, making the profession more attractive could require financial incentives, particularly for teachers of subjects such as mathematics and physics. He says such measures could encourage more graduates of teacher-training faculties to enter the profession. Data from Alma Career Slovakia, the country’s largest provider of job-search products and employee education services, shows that demand is currently strongest for lower-secondary teachers. On average, eight applicants respond to each teaching vacancy. However, Alma Career Slovakia PR manager Ľubica Melcerová explains schools are seeing much stronger interest in non-teaching positions. According to her vacancies for teaching assistants, cleaners and other support staff, including kitchen workers, attract between 40 and 60 applications on average. Source: STVR
